title: American Prisons Restrict Free Speech
author: Jack Verrill
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/04/Screenshot-2026-04-17-at-7.29.58-AM.png)

Photo: South Carolina Department of Corrections.

Over the span of a single week at the end of March, a Michigan prisoner was
[found dead](https://www.cbsnews.com/detroit/news/michigan-inmate-found-dead-
in-prison-cell-bellamy-creek-correctional-facility/) inside his cell in what
authorities are investigating as a homicide, [two inmates
died](https://www.newsnationnow.com/us-news/northeast/rikers-island-inmate-
dies-in-custody-second-in-one-week/) inside New York City’s infamous Rikers
Island jail complex, and an inmate was
[killed](https://www.montereycountynow.com/blogs/news_blog/inmate-killed-in-
suspected-assault-at-monterey-county-
jail/article_fb096c5e-6961-4b32-b4ae-f74330a7f755.html) inside a California
jail.

The violence and abuse that is commonplace in American prisons is beginning to
draw national attention. That same week,  _The Marshall Project_ released its
[investigation](https://www.themarshallproject.org/2026/03/27/prison-sexual-
misconduct-bryan-bop) into systemic sexual abuse inside a Texas womens prison,
a civil rights [lawsuit](https://www.kgw.com/article/news/crime/federal-civil-
lawsuit-alleges-former-multnomah-county-corrections-deputy-sexually-assaulted-
inmate/283-12e9a8e4-5503-4125-9431-0b29518c5e63) was filed accusing an Oregon
corrections deputy of raping an inmate inside her cell, and the state of
California paid $1.9 million to settle a
[lawsuit](https://www.kqed.org/news/12077737/california-agrees-
to-1-9m-settlement-in-prison-use-of-force-case) against jail staff accused of
excessive use of force. The American prison system is in a crisis of
accountability. Until state legislatures take measures to protect the speech
rights of prison inmates, incarceration will become an unspoken death sentence
for more American citizens.

Last year, filmmakers Andrew Jarecki and Charlotte Kaufman brought us into the
heart of this crisis. Their documentary, [ _The Alabama
Solution_](https://thealabamasolution.com/), uses smuggled cell phones to
document abuses inside Alabama state prisons. The documentary-style
investigation found over [1300
deaths](https://thealabamasolution.com/investigation-overview/) inside Alabama
prisons since 2019, less than half of which were of natural causes. One
family, whose son was beaten to death by prison guards, [was allegedly
told](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IuzYbR7Tn8c&pp=ygUdYWxhYm1hIHNvbHV0aW9uIGRlbW9jYXJjeSBub3c%3D)
that if they contacted reporters, his body would not be returned to them.
Another family [received their son’s body](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-
news/body-alabama-inmate-found-dead-prison-was-returned-family-heart-missin-
rcna129737) from prison officials with his heart missing after the family
commissioned a private autopsy.

As of 2025, [45%](https://www.prisonpolicy.org/reports/pie2025.html) of
Americans have an immediate family member who at some point was incarcerated,
most of them will never be featured in an award-winning documentary. In order
to prevent, investigate, and prosecute prison abuses, we need to know about
them in the first place. While a trio of 20th century Supreme Court
[decisions](https://www.cjr.org/united_states_project/first-amendment-
reporters-jail.php) grant prison officials discretion in barring media access
behind bars, [inmates still retain the right to free
speech,](https://www.freedomforum.org/prison-first-
amendment/#:~:text=First%20Amendment%20free%20speech%20and,order%20and%20security%20in%20prison.)
so long as it doesn’t legitimately jeopardize prison security. Doubling down
on free speech behind bars will make America’s jails and prisons safer.

In many cases of prison abuse, it is the victims who are punished instead of
the perpetrators. In its investigation into sexual misconduct in Texas
prisons,  _The Marshall Project_ notes how inmates and staff who spoke out
were threatened, one of the victims was even moved to a more restrictive
facility after reporting her sexual abuse. Likewise, when the initial media
buzz surrounding  _The Alabama Solution_ quieted, three inmates most critical
to the film were [placed into solitary
confinement](https://deadline.com/2026/01/inmates-in-the-alabama-solution-
moved-to-solitary-confinement-1236703191/). Filmmaker Charlotte Kaufman
explains, “What’s so disturbing is that [state prison officials] don’t have to
give a ‘why.’ They can… take away all of their belongings, cut them off from
their family members, cut them off from the outside world.”

This can even be done to well-resourced inmates. Last year, billion-dollar
crypto fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried was [placed in solitary confinement after
conducting](https://nypost.com/2025/03/08/us-news/sam-bankman-fried-gets-
solitary-after-unauthorized-jailhouse-interview-report/) an “un-authorized”
interview. You don’t even need to be convicted of a crime to find yourself in
solitary. In 2021, D.C. jail officials decided that all accused January 6th
[Capitol rioters would be housed in
solitary.](https://www.politico.com/news/2021/04/19/capitol-riot-defendants-
warren-483125) Forced to eat off the floor, they were locked in their cells
23-hours a day, given one hour daily to shower, exercise, and meet with their
attorneys.

Fortunately for those inmates, reporters latched on to their stories.  _The
Alabama Solution_ filmmakers launched a
[website](https://www.nomorealabama.com/take-action) for viewers to sign an
open letter, call Alabama correctional facilities, and donate directly to
inmates. Sam Bankman-Fried is [now in a low-
security](https://fortune.com/crypto/2025/04/10/sam-bankman-fried-sbf-ftx-
victorville-california-oklahoma-brooklyn/) California prison, and all accused
January 6th rioters were
[pardoned](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/trump-pardons-or-commutes-
terms-of-all-jan.-6-rioters) by President Donald Trump. Transparency, in those
cases, led to action.

But not everyone has a film crew, million-dollar legal funds, or the president
of the United States to advocate for them. Thankfully, state legislatures can
take practical legal action to defend prisoners’ speech rights behind bars.
This begins with making jailhouse phone calls free of charge. The Prison
Policy Initiative
[notes](https://www.prisonpolicy.org/phones/appendices2022_5.html) that a
15-minute phone call costs anywhere from 93 cents in New Jersey to $5.47 in
Minnesota. A significant price for inmates making [less than $1 per
hour](https://www.prisonpolicy.org/blog/2017/04/10/wages/) at their prison
jobs.

Facilities should also allow some inmates to have cell phones and social media
accounts of their own. It is reasonable for many non-violent offenders to
communicate freely with the outside world. Social media is a particularly
effective way to do this, yet in most cases is strictly forbidden. For
example, the South Carolina Department of Corrections considers inmates
“creating and/or assisting with a social networking site” a [Level 1
offense](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2015/02/hundreds-south-carolina-
inmates-sent-solitary-confinement-over-facebook) — putting it in the same
category as murder, rape, and hostage-taking.

In our 21st-century media ecosystem, there is no reason for prisons to be
information black holes. What happened last week, can happen next week, which
is why we need transparency today. Doubling down on prisoners’ First Amendment
rights is the best way to do it.
